transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thanks for seeing me. Um, well, I guess I'm here because I just... I can't seem to get anything done, and it's really starting to mess up my life. Since I don't have a job right now, my main focus is supposed to be finding one, but the main thing is I just get completely pulled off track by, well, literally every little sound or thought that pops into my head. It's actually exhausting. 

For example, yesterday—or maybe it was Tuesday, I don't know, the days kind of blend together lately—but I'll be sitting at my computer, right? Trying to work on a job application. Just a standard online application. And I'll be reading the first question, and then a car drives by outside. Not even a loud car, just regular street traffic, but my brain immediately locks onto that sound. And then my phone screen lights up with a notification out of the corner of my eye, and maybe it's just a spam email or a text, but I have to look at it. Or I'll just get some totally random idea, like wondering what happened to an actor from a movie I watched ten years ago, and suddenly I'm looking that up, and it just sends me somewhere else entirely before I even notice I stopped filling out the application. I'll look at the clock and realize an hour has passed and I haven't typed a single word. It just happens over and over and over again, all day long, and it's like my brain just refuses to stay where I want it to...
Do you often feel restless or fidgety when you're sitting still?

Yeah, absolutely. It's like I can't just... exist in a chair. Like, if I'm sitting with someone, maybe just hanging out or, I don't know, waiting for an appointment or something, my leg is usually bouncing. Like, bouncing a mile a minute. I don't even know I'm doing it until someone points it out, or if they put their hand on my knee to stop it, which my mom used to do all the time when I was younger, and honestly, some of my friends still do. And if it's not my leg, it's my hands. I'm always clicking a pen—click, click, click—which I know drives people crazy, or I'm digging in my pocket and messing with my keys, just jingling them around, or peeling the label off a water bottle until it's completely shredded. It's just... I don't even realize I'm doing it most of the time. It's like my body has all this extra energy that has to leak out somehow, and if I try to force myself to sit completely still, it almost physically hurts. Like this weird tension builds up in my chest and my arms, and I just have to move something, anything, just to feel normal. So yeah, I'm pretty much always fidgeting with something.
Does this happen to you at home, when you're alone, as well as when you're in other environments, like here or with friends?

Yeah, it's definitely everywhere. It's not just when I'm out or around other people, it's... it's really bad at home, too. Honestly, maybe even worse at home because there's nobody there to tell me to stop or give me that look, you know? Like, I used to play a ton of soccer, right? All through high school and for a few years after, I'd play in these pickup leagues, and I think that burned off a lot of the energy. But I messed up my ankle a while back, and since I can't play like I used to, sitting around the house is just... it's unbearable. It literally feels like I'm crawling out of my skin. 

I'll try to sit on the couch and watch a movie or even just scroll on my phone, and within ten minutes, I just can't take it. I have to get up. So I end up just pacing. I'll pace from the living room into the kitchen, maybe open the fridge, stare at it, not even want anything, close it, and then pace down the hallway to my bedroom, look out the window, and then turn around and pace right back to the living room. Over and over. My downstairs neighbor actually banged on the ceiling with a broom once because I guess I was pacing so heavy late at night. It's just this constant need to be moving, and when I'm alone in my apartment with no job to go to and no soccer to play, it's like the walls are closing in if I don't keep my feet moving. So yeah, home, here, everywhere... it never really turns off.
Do you often act on impulse without thinking through the consequences?

Impulse... like, doing things without thinking? Um, no, honestly, I don't really think I do that. I mean, it depends on what you mean by impulsive, I guess? Because when I hear that word, I think of people who just, like, go out and buy a whole new car on a whim, or, I don't know, suddenly decide to move across the country with no plan. And that is definitely not me. 

Honestly, right now, since I'm out of work, I have to be pretty careful with my money anyway, so it's not like I'm out there making wild purchases or anything like that. I actually kind of overthink things a lot of the time, or at least I get stuck in my head. Like my friend Mark, he's the type who will just randomly decide to go on a road trip or get a tattoo at two in the morning, and I'm always the one looking at him like he's crazy. I don't really take risks like that. 

I mean, sure, I'll get distracted and end up reading about some random movie star for an hour instead of filling out a job application, like I was saying earlier, but I wouldn't call that acting on impulse, you know? It's more just my brain wandering off. I don't do things that have, like, bad consequences or anything dangerous. I'm mostly just pacing around my apartment or bouncing my leg, feeling stuck. So, yeah, I don't think I do things without thinking them through. If anything, I think too much about what I'm supposed to be doing and just... can't do it. But no, no reckless stuff.
Do you often find yourself making careless mistakes when you're trying to focus on something?

Yeah, I do. I really do. And it's so frustrating because it's not like I don't know what I'm doing, you know? It's just... these stupid, tiny little things that slip right past me. Like, okay, so I've been looking into this automotive training program, right? Trying to get some kind of certification so I can actually get a decent job, maybe work in a garage, because I like cars and I figure, you know, it's hands-on, maybe I won't go crazy sitting at a desk. 

But anyway, I was filling out the application forms for it the other day, and there's all this paperwork. Pages of it. And I'm trying to focus, I really am. I'm sitting at my kitchen table, I've got my pen, I've got my coffee, I'm trying to do everything right. But I'll be going down the page, filling in my info, and I'll just completely skip a box. Like, my eyes just slide right over it. Or I'll be looking at a parts list online, trying to compare prices for this old Honda Civic my buddy is trying to fix up—I told him I'd help him figure out what he needs—and I'll write down a part number, but I'll transpose two of the digits. Like, it's supposed to be 8-4-9, and I'll write 8-9-4. 

And I don't even realize I did it until later when I'm trying to look the part up again and it says "item not found," or when the training program emails me back and says, "Hey, you missed section three." And then I just feel so incredibly dumb. Because I knew the information! It's not like I didn't know my own zip code or didn't know how to read a number off a screen. I just... my brain just glitches, I guess? It's like I'm moving too fast, even when I'm trying to go slow. I'll read over a sentence three times to make sure I didn't make a mistake, and I'll still miss that I spelled my own street name wrong. It happens all the time. It makes me feel like I can't trust my own eyes when I'm doing paperwork or anything detailed like that. It's just really embarrassing, honestly.
Do you find it hard to finish tasks because you lose interest or get bored before they're completed?

Hard to finish things? No, not really. I mean, I guess it depends on what you consider a task, right? But honestly, I wouldn't say I just get bored and stop. Like, take that automotive training program I was talking about. Sure, I mess up the forms sometimes, but I don't just walk away from it because I'm bored. I'm actually really interested in it. I want to get it done. 

If anything, I think my problem is more that I can't start things, or I get sidetracked by all those little mistakes I mentioned before, not that I just lose interest halfway through. Like, if I'm helping my buddy with his Civic, I'll stay out in the garage with him for hours. We'll be under the hood, hands covered in grease, trying to figure out why the idle is so rough, and I don't get bored at all. I'll actually get really into it, looking up forums on my phone, trying to see if anyone else had the same issue with that specific year and model. I'll go down a whole rabbit hole about vacuum leaks or whatever. 

So it's not a lack of interest. I don't just drop a wrench and say, "I'm bored, I'm going inside." It's more... I don't know, it's just the sitting still and doing the boring paperwork stuff that's hard, but even then, I try to push through it. I don't just quit. I just end up pacing around or getting frustrated with myself for making careless errors. But as far as just losing interest and abandoning things? No, I don't think that's really me. I try to see things through, especially if it's something I care about, like cars or trying to get my life on track. It's just the execution that gets messy, you know?
Have you noticed your symptoms affecting your relationships with friends or family?

Affecting my relationships? Um, no, I really haven't noticed anything like that. I mean, my family and friends, they just kind of know how I am, you know? Take my mom, for instance. She lives about forty minutes away, over in the next county, and I usually go see her on Sundays. Well, mostly Sundays, unless I get caught up helping Mark or something. But she never really complains about my behavior or anything like that. I mean, sure, she worries because I don't have a job right now, which makes sense, any mom would worry about that. She calls me to check if I've heard back from any of those applications—the ones I was telling you I keep messing up the paperwork for—but she doesn't get mad at me for being distracted or whatever. She just tells me to keep my head up and keep trying. 

And then with my friends, like Mark, the guy with the Honda Civic I mentioned earlier, we get along totally fine. We've actually been friends since high school. Tenth grade, I think it was, because we had shop class together and just hit it off. He knows I can be a little all over the place. Like, if we're hanging out watching a football game at his place, I usually can't just sit on the couch the whole time. I have to keep getting up, maybe go to the kitchen for water, or just stand by the back door for a minute because my legs feel restless. But he doesn't care at all. He's super laid back. Sometimes I'll talk his ear off for an hour about some random car part I was researching, and he just listens or laughs and tells me I am overthinking it. 

So, yeah, I haven't had any big arguments or lost any friends or anything. I'm not a difficult person to get along with, I just have all this nervous energy and I get stuck in my own head sometimes. But my circle is pretty small anyway, just a few close buddies and my family, and we are all completely solid. It definitely hasn't caused any real problems with them.
Do you often experience intense mood swings?

Intense mood swings? Um, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, what do you even consider an intense mood swing, really? Because to me, that sounds like someone who goes from being super happy to just suddenly screaming or crying for absolutely no reason, and that's definitely not me. I'm a pretty even-keeled guy for the most part, you know? 

I mean, sure, I get frustrated. Like I was saying earlier about that application for the automotive program—when I miss a box or mess up a number, I get mad at myself. I'll be sitting there at the kitchen table, and maybe I'll swear or toss my pen down, because it's just so incredibly annoying when I'm trying so hard and I still make a dumb mistake. But I feel like that's just... that's just normal frustration, right? Anybody would get annoyed if they were trying to do something important and kept messing up the stupid little details. 

But it doesn't last. It's not like that frustration ruins my whole day or makes me depressed or anything. Give me five minutes, maybe I'll go pace around the kitchen or grab a glass of water, and I'm totally fine again. I'm right back to normal. And it's definitely not like I just wake up feeling miserable out of nowhere. My mom always says I've got a pretty good disposition, even when things are stressful—like right now with not having a job and trying to figure out my next step. I try to keep positive about it all. 

So, yeah, no wild emotional rollercoasters or anything like that. Just the regular day-to-day stuff. Like, if a bolt is completely rusted on Mark's Civic and I bust my knuckles trying to wrench it off, I'll definitely yell, but I'm not, like, having a breakdown over it. I don't really have those big swings you're talking about.
Do you think your difficulties with staying focused and being easily distracted are more problematic for you than your restlessness and fidgeting?

Which one is more problematic? Hmm, that's a tough one to answer, honestly. Because, well, they both kind of mess with me in different ways, you know? It's hard to weigh them against each other like that. 

Like, the focus thing, the getting distracted—that's definitely a huge pain. Especially right now with the job stuff and the automotive program paperwork. I'll sit down with the best intentions, I've got my coffee, I've got my pen, and I'm like, "Okay, I'm going to get this application done today." And then, I don't know, a car drives by playing loud music, or I remember I need to check if that one specific socket wrench set is on sale at Harbor Freight, and suddenly I'm on my phone looking at tools for twenty minutes, and I completely lost my train of thought on the application. That's the part that makes me feel like I'm stuck, like I can't move forward with my life because I keep tripping over my own brain. It's incredibly frustrating.

But then, on the other hand, the restlessness is always there, too. It's like this constant hum in the background. Like I was saying about hanging out at Mark's place—I literally cannot just sit on the couch and watch a whole game. My legs start to feel like they're buzzing, like I have to move them or I'm going to jump out of my skin. And even when I'm trying to do the paperwork, part of the reason I get distracted is because sitting still at the kitchen table feels like torture after about ten minutes. I start bouncing my knee, then I'm tapping my pen, and then I just have to get up and pace around the kitchen island. 

So, I don't know if I can say one is definitely worse than the other. They kind of feed into each other, I think. The restlessness makes it harder to focus, and the lack of focus makes me more aware of how restless I am. If I had to pick which one has more real-world consequences right now, I guess maybe the focus issues, just because it's actively getting in the way of me getting into that training program. But the fidgeting and the pacing, that's just exhausting to live with every single day. So, yeah, I really couldn't pick a clear winner between the two. They're both just kind of a package deal for me.
Did you experience these difficulties with focus and restlessness when you were a kid?

As a kid? Oh, yeah. Yeah, absolutely. This definitely isn't a new thing for me at all. I mean, if you ask my mom, she'd probably have a million stories for you. But just from what I remember, even way back in elementary school, it was always an issue. I was that kid where the teachers were always, always moving my seat. It felt like every other week I was getting relocated. They'd put me right up front by the chalkboard, or sometimes they'd stick me all the way in the back corner by the bookshelves, just trying to find a spot where I wouldn't be a distraction to the rest of the class. 

Because I was constantly talking out of turn. Like, I just couldn't hold it in. If the teacher asked a question, I'd just blurt out the answer before she even called on anybody, or I'd turn around and start talking to whoever was behind me about something totally unrelated, like a cartoon I watched that morning or whatever. I just always had something to say and no filter to stop it.

And the schoolwork part was a total mess, too. I was always forgetting my homework. I'd either forget to write down what the assignment even was, or I'd actually manage to do it at home and then just leave it sitting on the kitchen table. Or it would end up completely crumpled at the bottom of my backpack under a bunch of old permission slips. My mom used to get so stressed trying to help me keep my folders organized. 

And then when we had to do in-class stuff, like those worksheets where you have to do a bunch of math problems or fill in the blanks? I would just rush right through them. I just wanted to be done, you know? I couldn't stand sitting there staring at the paper, so I'd speed through the whole thing and end up making all these really careless mistakes. I'd add instead of subtract, or I'd just completely skip a whole row of questions because my eyes were jumping all over the page. It wasn't that I didn't know how to do the work, I wasn't stupid, I just... I couldn't slow my brain down enough to do it right. So, yeah, this whole thing with the focus and the restlessness, it's been exactly like this pretty much as far back as I can remember.
Did your parents or teachers ever take you to see a doctor or a specialist when you were a kid because of these issues with focus and restlessness?

No, you know, it's actually kind of funny you ask that, because looking back, you'd really think someone would have suggested it, right? But no, I never went to a doctor or a specialist or a counselor or anything like that when I was little. My mom... well, she just kind of chalked it all up to me being a high-energy kid. She’d always say, "Oh, he’s just got ants in his pants," or "He’s just all boy." That was her absolute favorite excuse for me, "he's all boy." 

And the teachers—I mean, they complained a ton, obviously. Like I was saying about moving my desk all over the place, and there were so many parent-teacher conferences where they’d tell my mom I just needed to "apply myself" more. I actually remember this one teacher, Mrs. Gable in fourth grade? She kept a literal notebook of every single time I talked out of turn or got out of my seat during quiet reading time. She brought it out at open house and showed it to my mom, and my mom was so embarrassed she grounded me from riding my bike for like two weeks. But even with all of that, with the notebook and the constant desk moving, nobody ever actually sat down and said, "Hey, maybe you should take him to a pediatrician to get checked out." 

It was always just framed as a discipline thing, you know? Or a maturity issue. They all just told my mom I'd grow out of it eventually once I got to middle school or high school. Which, I mean, spoiler alert, I definitely didn't grow out of it, considering I'm sitting right here talking to you about it at twenty-six. But yeah, back then, at least at my school, they didn't really rush to send you to a doctor unless you were doing something really crazy. They just gave me extra detention, or my gym teacher would make me run extra laps to try and burn off the energy. So... no. No doctors back then. Just a whole lot of getting in trouble and hoping I'd calm down on my own.
Do you think your difficulties with staying focused or your restlessness and fidgeting cause you more problems in your daily life?

I guess, like I was kind of touching on earlier when you asked about this, the focus stuff is really what's throwing a massive wrench in my actual life plans right now. The restlessness is super annoying to live with, sure, but the lack of focus? It's literally keeping me from getting my life together. 

Like I mentioned, I've been trying to get into this automotive technician training program. And the absolute most frustrating part of this whole situation is that I know—I absolutely *know*—that I can handle the hands-on work. Once I'm in a garage, under a hood, getting my hands dirty? I'm golden. I helped my buddy rebuild a carburetor last summer and it was like my brain just completely clicked into place, you know? I get how parts fit together. But getting to that point... it's just a complete nightmare. 

Because I can't stay focused on the boring administrative stuff, I’ve actually missed the official training deadlines. Like, hard, non-negotiable deadlines to submit all the enrollment paperwork. I'll sit down to start the application, get distracted by literally anything—like I was saying about looking up tools online—and then suddenly I look at the calendar and it's three days past the due date. And then, because I missed it, I have to wait for the next enrollment period and start the whole process over, which means redoing applications I already half-finished. I've had to redo the exact same forms so many times because I either lose them, forget to hit submit on the online portal, or I fill out the wrong section because my eyes are just bouncing around the page and I'm not reading the instructions right. 

So I'm just... I'm stuck. I'm twenty-six and I’m still not moving forward toward becoming an automotive technician, all because I can't just sit down and focus on a stupid piece of paper for twenty uninterrupted minutes. It’s incredibly frustrating because the ability is there, the drive to do the actual job is there, but the execution on the paperwork is just non-existent. So, yeah, if we're talking about what's causing the biggest actual roadblocks and messing up my daily life, it's definitely the focus problems.
Did you experience significant difficulties with focus, restlessness, or fidgeting consistently throughout your childhood?

Well, I know I just talked your ear off about how I was always moving desks and getting in trouble as a kid, so the baseline stuff—the ants in the pants—that was definitely always there. But if you're asking if it was *consistently* this much of a nightmare, like, completely ruining my life every single day since I was seven? No, not really. I mean, I found ways to cope as I got older, I guess, or at least I managed to scrape by. 

But as far as it being *this* disruptive, where I literally can't get my life together or fill out a basic form? That's actually a lot more recent. It’s been this disruptive for about a year and ten months. I know the exact timeline, honestly, because it's ever since my soccer injury. 

See, I used to play in this local adult rec league, right? Every Tuesday and Thursday night we had practice, plus actual games on the weekends. It was a whole schedule. And it was great for me because it kept me constantly moving, it burned off all that crazy physical energy I always have, and it gave my entire week this really solid, predictable structure. Like, I knew exactly what I was doing and when I had to do it. But then, yeah, about a year and ten months ago, I went in for this really aggressive slide tackle during a tournament, completely messed up my knee, and that was it. Season over. 

I was stuck on the couch resting it for weeks, and it just completely knocked me out of my usual routine. And I didn't realize how much I was relying on that routine until it was gone. Once that schedule disappeared, it was like my brain just completely short-circuited. Without the soccer to anchor my week, I couldn't focus on *anything*, the restlessness got a thousand times worse because I couldn't just go run it off on the pitch, and suddenly I couldn't even keep track of what day it was. That's when all the paperwork for the mechanic program started falling through the cracks. So, yeah, the fidgeting and stuff was there when I was little, absolutely, but this absolute roadblock level of it? That's just been the last year and ten months, ever since that injury took away my routine.
Did you have any of these focus or restlessness issues prior to the age of 12?

Yeah, absolutely. Like I was kind of saying earlier with Mrs. Gable and the notebook in fourth grade, that was all way before I was twelve. I mean, elementary school was basically just one long game of musical chairs for me because the teachers were always moving my seat. They’d put me right up front by the chalkboard so they could watch me, but then I’d just talk out of turn and interrupt them constantly, so then they’d get fed up and move me to the back corner. But then I'd just distract whoever was back there with me! 

But, you know, it wasn't just the talking and the fidgeting that started back then, the focus stuff was totally there too, even if it wasn't ruining my life the way it is now. Like, I was absolutely notorious for forgetting my homework. It was a whole thing. I would actually do the assignment at home sometimes, but then I'd leave it on the kitchen table, or it would somehow end up crumpled into this unrecognizable wad at the very bottom of my backpack under my gym shoes. 

And when we had in-class stuff? Forget about it. I just wanted to be done so I could go to recess or draw engines in my notebook, so I would just completely rush through all the worksheets. I wasn't even reading the instructions half the time. I'd just blast through it and make the most ridiculous, careless mistakes. My mom used to get so frustrated because she knew I wasn't stupid, but my math sheets would come back covered in red ink just because I was rushing so fast I’d add instead of subtract, or I'd skip entire sections of the page. So, yeah, long before I was twelve... the blurting things out, the lost homework, the botched worksheets, all of it was happening right there in elementary school.
Did you experience significant symptoms of inattention, such as making careless mistakes or having difficulty sustaining attention, prior to the age of 7?

Man, before age seven? That's... I mean, you're asking me to go way back in the vault there. Seven is what, like, first grade? Maybe kindergarten? I know I just went on and on about fourth grade and all the elementary school stuff, and I definitely remember that era because that's when you actually have to sit down and do real worksheets, you know? You get graded, the teachers are actually watching your performance. 

But before seven... I honestly couldn't tell you. My memories from back then are just a bunch of random, fuzzy flashes. Like, I remember playing in the dirt a lot, or this one time I ate a blue crayon in kindergarten because my older brother convinced me it would taste like blueberries—which it absolutely did not, by the way, it was awful. But as far as making careless mistakes on things or not sustaining attention? I don't even know what I would have been paying attention *to* back then. It's mostly just finger painting and building blocks and nap time, right? 

If I was making careless mistakes, like, coloring outside the lines or whatever, nobody really brought it up or made a big deal out of it. My mom always just said I was a "spirited" little kid, always running around the yard, but she never really mentioned me having trouble focusing on actual tasks before I started proper, sit-down school. So, yeah, I really don't have a good answer for you on that one. It's just kind of a blank spot, honestly. I mean, how much does anyone really remember from being five or six anyway? You're just kind of existing and running on pure sugar and Saturday morning cartoons, so I really can't say if I was having focus issues back then.
Did you have any problems with focus, restlessness, or fidgeting before you were 12 years old that your parents or teachers noticed?

Yeah, I mean, like I was saying before, it was definitely a thing way before I was twelve. It's funny you ask about teachers noticing, because, man, they definitely noticed. I feel like I was a permanent fixture on their radar. Elementary school for me was just this endless cycle of getting my desk moved. 

Like, Mrs. Gable in fourth grade, I swear she moved my desk every other week. First, I'd be up in the very front row, right under her nose, because she thought that would keep me focused, right? But then I'd just be blurting things out, answering questions before she even finished asking them, or I'd turn around and start talking to the kid behind me because I was bored. So then she'd get frustrated and banish me to the back corner of the room. But that was even worse because then I had a full view of the whole class and I'd just find someone else to distract, or I'd be tipping my chair back, tapping my pencil, just constantly fidgeting. 

And it wasn't just the moving around and the talking, either. The focus stuff was a huge issue for them too. My homework was a disaster zone. I was always forgetting it. Like, I’d actually sit down and do it at home—well, sometimes—but then it would just vanish. I’d leave it on the kitchen counter, or it would get shoved into the abyss of my backpack and come out looking like an accordion three weeks later. The teachers were constantly sending notes home about missing assignments. 

And when we did work in class? Oh man, I would just tear through it. I hated sitting there doing worksheets, so I would just rush through them as fast as humanly possible so I could go do something else, like draw in the margins or look out the window. And because I was rushing so much, I wasn't even reading the instructions properly. I'd make the dumbest, most careless mistakes. Like on math tests, I'd add instead of subtract, or I'd just completely skip the back page of a worksheet because I didn't even flip it over. My mom and my teachers used to have these long conferences about it because they knew I understood the material, but my grades were always taking a hit because I just couldn't slow down and pay attention to what I was actually doing. So, yeah, the teachers and my parents were definitely, definitely noticing all of that way before I hit middle school.
How old were you when you first started experiencing difficulties with focus and restlessness?

I mean, I feel like I'm kind of a broken record here, doc, but—and I know we literally just went over all the Mrs. Gable stuff and the homework disasters—but if you're looking for an exact age... I guess I'd say probably around eight or nine? Like, third or fourth grade is when it really, really became obvious to everyone. 

Because, like I was saying, even in elementary school, the teachers were always moving my seat. It was basically a weekly ritual. They just didn't know what to do with me because I talked out of turn so much, and I was constantly forgetting my homework, and just... absolutely rushing through those worksheets and making all those careless mistakes. I just didn't have the patience to sit there and do it the way they wanted me to. 

So, yeah, as soon as I was old enough to be in a real classroom where they actually expected you to sit quietly in rows and do graded work—so, you know, eight or nine years old—that's when all this focus and restlessness stuff really blew up. Before that, like I said about kindergarten, it was mostly just playing and running around, but the second the real academic expectations started in elementary school, all those issues with my attention and fidgeting were right there front and center.
Do you think your difficulties with focus and restlessness are more consistent with the inattentive type, the hyperactive-impulsive type, or a combination of both?

Man, I don't even know what all those official types mean, to be completely honest with you. Like, inattentive, hyperactive... it all just feels like one big giant tangled mess in my head, you know? It's not like I wake up on a Tuesday and go, well, today I'm feeling the inattentive thing, and then Wednesday I'm suddenly the hyperactive guy. It's just... it's just my life. It's all happening at the exact same time, basically all the time. 

Like, if I'm sitting there supposed to be paying attention to someone talking—or, well, back when I was in school, or even just trying to watch a movie now—my brain is just completely checked out, drifting off to wherever. Which I guess is that inattentive part you're talking about? But at the exact same moment my brain is checked out, my leg is bouncing up and down like a jackhammer under the table, or I'm chewing on the inside of my cheek, or I'm feeling this crazy, unbearable urge to just stand up and pace around the room for absolutely no reason. So is that the hyperactive part? Or is that just me trying to physically force myself to stay awake because I'm not paying attention? It's totally a chicken and egg situation, doc. I really couldn't tell you which one is driving the bus. 

And honestly, my mom used to say I had a motor attached to me, but in the exact same breath, she’d say I was completely off in my own little world, ignoring everyone. So if you're asking me to pick one of those specific types out of a lineup, I really couldn't do it. I don't know the medical boxes you guys use for this stuff. I just know that I can't focus on anything to save my life, and I also can't sit still while I'm failing to focus on it. As a kid? Oh, yeah. Yeah, absolutely. This definitely isn't a new thing for me at all. I mean, if you ask my mom, she'd probably have a million stories for you. They'd put me right up front by the chalkboard, or sometimes they'd stick me all the way in the back corner by the bookshelves, just trying to find a spot where I wouldn't be a distraction to the rest of the class. 

Because I was constantly talking out of turn. Like, I just couldn't hold it in. If the teacher asked a question, I'd just blurt out the answer before she even called on anybody, or I'd turn around and start talking to whoever was behind me about something totally unrelated, like a cartoon I watched that morning or whatever. I'd either forget to write down what the assignment even was, or I'd actually manage to do it at home and then just leave it sitting on the kitchen table. And then when we had to do in-class stuff, like those worksheets where you have to do a bunch of math problems or fill in the blanks? I would just rush right through them. I'd add instead of subtract, or I'd just completely skip a whole row of questions because my eyes were jumping all over the page. Which, I mean, spoiler alert, I definitely didn't grow out of it, considering I'm sitting right here talking to you about it at twenty-six. But yeah, back then, at least at my school, they didn't really rush to send you to a doctor unless you were doing something really crazy. But as far as it being *this* disruptive, where I literally can't get my life together or fill out a basic form? That's actually a lot more recent. It’s been this disruptive for about a year and ten months. I know the exact timeline, honestly, because it's ever since my soccer injury. 

See, I used to play in this local adult rec league, right? Every Tuesday and Thursday night we had practice, plus actual games on the weekends. It was a whole schedule. And it was great for me because it kept me constantly moving, it burned off all that crazy physical energy I always have, and it gave my entire week this really solid, predictable structure. Like, I knew exactly what I was doing and when I had to do it. But then, yeah, about a year and ten months ago, I went in for this really aggressive slide tackle during a tournament, completely messed up my knee, and that was it. Season over. 

I was stuck on the couch resting it for weeks, and it just completely knocked me out of my usual routine. And I didn't realize how much I was relying on that routine until it was gone. Once that schedule disappeared, it was like my brain just completely short-circuited. Without the soccer to anchor my week, I couldn't focus on *anything*, the restlessness got a thousand times worse because I couldn't just go run it off on the pitch, and suddenly I couldn't even keep track of what day it was. That's when all the paperwork for the mechanic program started falling through the cracks. So, yeah, the fidgeting and stuff was there when I was little, absolutely, but this absolute roadblock level of it? That's just been the last year and ten months, ever since that injury took away my routine.
